name: Kanzuri (Myoko chili-koji paste)
text: A fermented chili seasoning from the Myoko area of Niigata. Sources describe it as Myoko chilies combined with rice koji, yuzu and sea salt, aged about three years. Salted chilies are laid out on snow in midwinter (yuki-sarashi) to draw out harshness before being ground and mixed. Tradition ties the chili to Uesugi Kenshin, but sources vary on the details of that story.
flavor: Deep, rounded heat with yuzu fragrance and a salty, fermented savoury note; much softer than fresh chili paste.
use: Dabbed on nabe, soba, sashimi, grilled fish and tofu, or dissolved into soup and sauces as a seasoning rather than eaten in quantity.
craft: The point is the sequence: autumn salting, snow exposure in the cold season (starting around Daikan according to one source), grinding, then mixing with rice koji, yuzu and salt and ageing about three years with a hand-turning (air-introducing) once a year. Some retail copy claims longer ageing, so check the maker's stated years. Judge by how integrated the heat is with koji sweetness and citrus, not by raw pungency.

name: Okinawa kokuto (Okinawa brown cane sugar)
text: Kokuto is a non-centrifugal (molasses-retaining) cane sugar made on Okinawa's outlying islands. The Okinawa kokuto cooperative defines it as pure kokuto: cane juice boiled and concentrated, then cooled with no other processing. It is listed in MAFF's geographical indication register (No. 172). Reported output for the 2024-25 season was about 8,800 t, and the cooperative's membership and island count are stated differently by different sources.
flavor: Dark, mineral and caramel-like, with a lingering sweetness and slight bitterness, varying by island and crush.
use: Eaten as lumps, melted into simmered dishes (kakuni, buta no kakuni-style braises), sweet sauces, dessert syrups and tea; also a base for kokuto shochu.
craft: Because nothing is removed, flavor depends on cane variety, harvest timing and how the juice is skimmed and boiled. Compare islands side by side rather than assuming one house flavor. Sweetness is less clean than refined sugar, so adjust sugar-to-soy balance in simmers and keep it away from delicate dishes where mineral notes would dominate.
src: MAFF GI register No. 172 - Okinawa kokuto
ALIC - Okinawa kokuto of eight islands

name: Kagoshima kokuto (Amami and island brown sugar)
text: MAFF's regional cuisine page describes kokuto as sugar made by cutting cane fine, pressing it, and boiling down the juice. In Kagoshima it is made on outlying islands such as Tokunoshima, Kikai, Amami-Oshima and Tanegashima, in small workshop-scale facilities. A source gives 2017-18 national kokuto output as 10,350 t, of which Okinawa 9,642 t and Kagoshima 708 t, so Kagoshima's share is small.
flavor: Rich molasses sweetness with mineral depth; character shifts with the island and the maker.
use: Eaten as it is, in sweets and tea, and as the base for Amami kokuto shochu and local simmered dishes.
craft: Small-scale boiling means batch variation is real; taste before standardising a recipe. Use where molasses tone is wanted (simmered pork, sweet-bean cooking), not as a drop-in for refined sugar.

name: Kamagari moshio (seaweed-salt revival)
text: Moshio is an ancient salt made with seaweed; its exact ancient method is not settled. At Kamagari in Hiroshima, the discovery of Kofun-period salt-making pottery during construction work prompted research. Matsuura Nobuhide traced the seaweed to hondawara via the Man'yoshu word tamamo. Sources describe soaking hondawara in seawater, draining and drying it, repeating this over 2-3 days to get strong brine, then boiling it in a kettle. One source also mentions filtering ash of burned seaweed with seawater.
flavor: Rounded, slightly sweet, with a faint marine, mineral note rather than sharp saltiness.
use: Finishing salt for sashimi, tempura, grilled fish and rice balls, where its softer salinity shows.
craft: Methods differ by maker (days of soaking, ash step, pot or kettle), so compare labels. Taste the same dish with plain salt to confirm what the seaweed actually adds before paying a premium.
src: Moshio no Kai - What is moshio

name: Hakata Salt Industry moshio (Saredo-shio)
ja: 伯方塩業 されど塩 藻塩
text: Hakata Salt Industry's moshio product is described as made using its flow-down, branch-trellis salt farm (ryuka-shiki edajika heiyo), then boiled in a flat pan (hiragama). It shows how a modern producer reinterprets the ancient seaweed salt within a seawater-concentration plant rather than by the old pottery method.
flavor: Soft, round salinity with a gentle sweetness from the seaweed.
use: Finishing and table salt; seasoning for vegetables, fish and rice.
craft: Ask the maker for the concentration method (trellis versus other) and the boiling vessel, and compare it with plain salt in the same dish before committing to a premium.
src: Hakata Salt Industry - history of Japanese salt-making

name: Taihaku sesame oil (unroasted sesame oil)
text: A sesame oil pressed from raw, unroasted seed, so it is nearly colourless with little aroma, unlike toasted brown sesame oil. Sources note it is used across Japanese and Western cooking and sweets because it is neutral. Kuki's Taihaku oil is described as pressed at low temperature without roasting. Methods differ by maker: some use pressing, others solvent extraction.
flavor: Neutral, clean, faintly nutty at most; no roasted perfume.
use: Tempura frying (as a base or blend), dressings, confectionery, and any dish where sesame flavor is not wanted.
craft: Check the label for pressed (assaku) versus extracted. Do not substitute toasted oil for it in frying where aroma and colour matter.
src: Fily - What is taihaku sesame oil
Kadoya Goma-lab - Brown vs white sesame oil

name: Assaku vs chushutsu (pressed vs solvent-extracted oil)
text: Pressed (assaku) oil is obtained by pressure alone without chemical solvents. Tamajime is a slow press method. Extracted (chushutsu) oil uses solvents such as hexane. Sources say a single first press (ichiban-shibori) preserves more aroma compounds than extraction. Sesame oil shows the contrast clearly, and taihaku can be made either way depending on the maker.
flavor: Pressed: fuller aroma and body; extracted: cleaner, more neutral.
use: Buy pressed oil for finishing and where aroma carries the dish; extracted oil is suitable for neutral frying.
craft: Read the process line on the label; the word 'taihaku' alone does not tell you the method.
src: Olive Hitomawashi - Pressed, tamajime and extracted sesame oil

name: Jozo-su grades under JAS (brewed vinegar)
text: Under the JAS standard for brewed vinegar, acidity is generally 4.0% or more. Grain vinegar (kokumotsu-su) needs 4.2% or more and at least 40 g of grain per litre; rice vinegar, brown-rice vinegar, black vinegar, kasu vinegar and malt vinegar fall here. Fruit vinegar needs 4.5% or more. Rice kurozu has an added total-nitrogen requirement of 0.12% or more.
flavor: Grain vinegars: soft and rounded; fruit vinegars: aromatic and sharper.
use: Use acidity and grade to calibrate sushi-meshi, awase-zu and pickling brines.
craft: Acidity differs among products, so measure when converting a recipe between brands. Grain content is a legal minimum, not a quality grade.
src: MAFF - JAS standard for brewed vinegar

name: Ponzu (citrus-vinegar dipping sauce)
text: Ponzu originally means citrus juice with vinegar, without soy sauce; one source derives 'pon' from a Dutch word for citrus juice. Today the soy-added ponzu-joyu is what people usually call ponzu. Home recipes combine soy sauce, citrus juice, vinegar or mirin, kombu and katsuobushi. The ratios quoted vary widely: soy to juice 1:1, 3:2 or 7:5, or 100 mL each of soy, juice and vinegar.
flavor: Bright acid, soy savoury depth and citrus perfume.
use: Dipping sauce for nabe, shabu-shabu, grilled fish, gyoza and chilled dishes.
craft: These sources are consumer recipe sites, not trade standards. Resting the sauce with kombu and katsuobushi, then straining, is the usual step. Adjust acid to the citrus you have, since yuzu, sudachi, kabosu and daidai differ.

name: Wagarashi (Japanese mustard)
text: Wagarashi is made from ground seed of oriental mustard (karashi-na) and is hotter than western mustard. The powder is mixed with water or warm water and kneaded; the enzyme myrosinase acts during mixing to produce the pungent compound. Western mustard typically adds sugar, vinegar or wine and uses white, brown or black mustard seed. Tube karashi often has vegetable fat and thickener added to stabilise pungency.
flavor: Sharp, nose-clearing heat with little sweetness.
use: Oden, tonkatsu, natto, shumai, and dressed greens (karashi-ae).
craft: Knead with warm water and rest briefly (covered) so pungency develops; use freshly made paste for the strongest effect. Classifications differ across sources (some use a three-way split of wagarashi, black and white).

name: Tenjitsu-en (solar salt)
text: Solar salt is made by bringing seawater into salt ponds and letting sun and wind evaporate it until crystals form, typically at large scale and slowly. Sources note Japan's humid, rainy climate and limited flat land made this hard domestically, so Japan developed boiling and concentration methods. The seawater is only about 3% salt.
flavor: Clean salinity; mineral character depends on the source water and the pond.
use: Base for blended or re-processed salt; used where large crystalline grain is wanted.
craft: Much solar salt is imported; check origin. Moisture and bittern content vary, so adjust weight when seasoning.

name: Ryuka-shiki edajika-heiyo salt farm
ja: 流下式枝条架併用塩田
text: The mainstream Japanese salt-making method from 1953 to 1971. Seawater is sprayed over branch trellises (edajika) so sun and wind evaporate it, producing concentrated brine that is then boiled. It replaced earlier sand-based salt farms and was in turn replaced by the ion-exchange membrane method.
flavor: Salt boiled from this brine is the base of some artisan salts.
use: Referenced for origin of flat-pan salts such as Hakata's.
craft: A few makers retain the trellis concentration step by choice; ask whether concentration is by trellis or membrane.
src: Hakata Salt Industry - History of Japanese salt-making

name: Saikan and senogo (brine collection and boiling)
text: The two basic steps of salt-making: saikan (collecting concentrated brine, kansui, from seawater) and senogo (boiling it to extract crystals). The ion-exchange membrane method, which concentrates seawater electrically, was developed in Japan independently and replaced salt farms. Agehama-shiki, sand-based concentration, goes back to the medieval period and continues in parts of the Noto Peninsula.
flavor: Not applicable (process term).
use: Used to ask makers how their salt is concentrated and how it is boiled.
craft: Ask both steps: concentration (trellis, sand, membrane, solar) and boiling (flat pan, vacuum, kettle) separately.
src: Shio Jigyo Center - History of Japanese salt-making

name: Hondawara (sargassum for moshio)
text: Hondawara is the sargassum-type seaweed identified for making moshio. In the Kamagari research, Matsuura Nobuhide linked the Man'yoshu term tamamo to hondawara. It is soaked in seawater, drained and dried repeatedly for 2-3 days to build a strong brine that is then boiled.
flavor: Adds a faint marine sweetness to salt.
use: Raw material for moshio; not eaten as the seasoning itself.
craft: Drying and soaking cycles, and whether the seaweed is also burned, differ by maker; the old method is not firmly documented.

name: Yuki-sarashi (snow-exposing chilies)
text: A step in kanzuri-making: chilies salted in autumn are spread on snow in the cold season for several days. Sources say the snow draws out harshness and salt and mellows the heat. The work begins around Daikan. The chilies are then ground and mixed with koji, yuzu and salt for ageing.
flavor: Process term; the result is rounder chili heat.
use: Explains the character of kanzuri.
craft: Timing depends on snowfall; the step is weather-dependent.

name: Shirashita-to (wasanbon intermediate)
text: The crystalline mass produced after cane juice is boiled, skimmed of scum and cooled; it is the raw material from which wasanbon is made. It is wrapped in cloth and pressed in an oshibune to drive out molasses, then kneaded with a little water (togi).
flavor: Process term.
use: Starting material for wasanbon.
craft: Careful skimming matters because the cane is rich in scum.

name: Oshibune and togi (wasanbon pressing and kneading)
text: Oshibune is the weighted press that squeezes liquid molasses out of cloth-wrapped shirashita-to. Togi is the hand kneading with a little water that follows. The pair is repeated roughly three to five times; the name wasanbon is said to come from repeating pressing and kneading three times, though that is stated as tradition.
flavor: Process term; result is fine, melt-in-mouth sugar.
use: Explains why wasanbon is fine-grained.
craft: Molasses is not removed completely; the maker's judgement sets the amount remaining.

name: Chikuto (bamboo cane for wasanbon)
text: Chikuto is the slender sugar cane variety used for wasanbon, distinct from the cane used for Okinawan kokuto. It is pressed and boiled with careful scum removal to make shirashita-to.
flavor: Delicate, clean sweetness in the finished sugar.
use: Raw material for wasanbon in Tokushima and Kagawa.
craft: Variety and handling shape the finish; ask the maker where the cane is grown.

name: Ichimi, shichimi and nanairo togarashi
ja: 一味・七味・七色唐辛子
text: Ichimi is chili alone. Shichimi has no strict definition: each shop has its own blend. One source says shichimi is mainly roasted chili powder while nanairo is mainly dried chili. Yawataya Isogoro's shichimi lists chili, sansho, ginger, hemp seed, sesame, chinpi and shiso. Yagenbori in Asakusa uses two chilies including roasted; Shichimiya Honpo in Kyoto uses aromatic non-chili ingredients.
flavor: Heat from chili, numbing from sansho, citrus and herbal notes from the rest.
use: Udon, soba, oyakodon, yakitori, soups.
craft: Compare blends for chili proportion and sansho level; store sealed and add at the table to keep aroma.

name: Kanmitsu-to (molasses-retaining sugar)
text: Sugar that keeps its cane molasses. Kokuto is the clearest example; Okinawa's cooperative restricts the name to cane juice boiled down with no other processing. Wasanbon is also described as leaving a measured amount of molasses, unlike refined white sugar, which removes it entirely.
flavor: Mineral, deeper sweetness.
use: Select kanmitsu-to when molasses flavor should be part of the dish.
craft: Amounts of molasses change both flavor and moisture, so adjust quantities when substituting for refined sugar.
